sources.title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood: Coding Agent Power Tools
sources.note: Full transcript plus episode README read.

sources.title: Loops Engineering from First Principles (Kyle Mistele)
Dev Interrupted: Dex Horthy on Ralph, RPI, and escaping the Dumb Zone
sources.note: No file was supplied in my bundle; not fetched. The ~$10-11/hour Ralph economics figure is not covered by any card.

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: LLM's amplifier of operator skill. Um and if you just set it off and run away
cards.claim: Dex argues unattended loop products will underperform because an LLM amplifies operator skill, so the loop must be babysat and tuned by someone curious about why it behaved as it did.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion stated at the start of the stream; supported by his own live runs.
cards.landing: Owner view / phase routine: loops need a named supervising human

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you really want to actually babysit this thing and then get really curious why it did that thing
cards.claim: Learning comes from watching the loop run (the 'fireplace') and tuning behaviour in or out, never blaming the model.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex streams runs and watches them on his phone; found the test-runner trick this way.
cards.landing: Phase routine: a watched first iteration of any new loop before going AFK

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Human on the loop is better than human in the loop
cards.claim: Position (Geoff voices it, Dex agrees): the human designs and steers the loop and may stop it at chosen points, while the model does not decide when and how.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated in conversation, no data.
cards.landing: Phase routine design: human gates at PR review, not per step

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I do have some concerns that people will just like try the official plugin
cards.claim: Dex criticises Anthropic's official Ralph plugin as not the real technique, since it keeps one session alive and relies on the model to emit a completion promise.
cards.evidence_detail: Side-by-side live comparison of the plugin against a plain bash loop.
cards.landing: Anything in-session (stop-hook loops) vs fresh-process loops

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: This is funny because it's all in one context window. It's just seeing its own context
cards.claim: Observed: the plugin run, in one context, repeated a done-checkmark for 110 iterations, while the fresh-start bash loop re-learns and finds new work.
cards.evidence_detail: Plugin hit iteration 110 with no completion promise; the stop hook kept firing on a finished project.
cards.landing: Verifier design: fresh context beats a self-assessing session (matches refuter pattern)

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: compaction is the devil
cards.claim: Geoff says, and Dex's setup follows, that auto-compaction is lossy and can drop the specs and goal, so the loop should never compact and should hold one goal per context window.
cards.evidence_detail: Explained on the whiteboard diagram; no measurement.
cards.landing: Context-budget policy: one phase per new session; avoid compaction

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: One context window, one activity, one goal
cards.claim: Each loop iteration sets exactly one objective and re-allocates the same fixed context (specs, plan) deterministically.
cards.evidence_detail: Whiteboard explanation; the prompt says 'implement the single highest priority feature'.
cards.landing: Phase routine: one phase per chat, fixed starting read-list

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Deliberate malicking context about your application.
cards.claim: Reserve roughly 5,000 tokens at the head of every iteration for what is being built, as an index or README of links to specs, injecting specific files by name when the model drifts.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as a rough budget; the 'vibes' are admitted.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md as a small index to specs; trim target

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: There is a dumb zone. You should stay out of it.
cards.claim: Leave headroom in each iteration for test failures and for committing and pushing, so the whole task, including the fix-up, fits in the smart zone.
cards.evidence_detail: Diagram of a performance-degradation line; position not given as a number in this video.
cards.landing: Phase sizing: size a phase so the closing steps (PR, journal) still fit

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Most test runners are trash. They output too many tokens.
cards.claim: Test output given to the agent should show only failing cases; the usual tail -100 or head -50 truncation hides errors at the other end and forces costly re-runs.
cards.evidence_detail: A script Allison and Claude built; Dex notes slow suites (hours) make re-runs expensive.
cards.landing: Backpressure scripts: a quiet-on-success test runner wrapper (pytest/jest/lint-imports)

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I did not put a push command in my prompt, and so the agents didn't push
cards.claim: Deterministic steps (push, commit, evaluate, git reset --hard) belong in the outer orchestrator script rather than the prompt, which makes them reliable.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's own agents failed to push in the live run; Geoff replies to do it in the orchestrator.
cards.landing: Hooks/scripts outside the model for commit, push and gate checks; re-opens the skipped hooks idea

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the idea of an orchestrator running chord code. So or running a harness.
cards.claim: Treat the loop as an outer harness around the inner harness: a supervisor loop can classify whether a thing was done (for example translations) and jump out to follow-up prompts.
cards.evidence_detail: Geoff describes it; Dex adopts the inner/outer harness framing.
cards.landing: Reusable workflow library: saved outer-harness scripts with a classify-then-nudge step

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if I tell you not to think about an elephant what are you thinking about
cards.claim: Negative instructions in the context prime the thing they forbid, so less in the context window is better and prompts should not scold the model.
cards.evidence_detail: Seen when the plugin run read the prompt and emitted the promise after the first item.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md wording: replace do-not rules with positive rules or deterministic checks

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: dangerously allow all is literally like put deliberately injecting humans into the loop
cards.claim: Unattended runs are acceptable only inside a disposable, network-restricted VM with no private data and a minimal credential set; assume it will be compromised and size the blast radius (lethal trifecta).
cards.evidence_detail: Two GCP VMs with only deploy keys and cloud API keys; Geoff voices the 'when it gets popped' line.
cards.landing: Permission policy for any unattended run: sandbox VM, scoped deploy keys, no prod secrets

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can just kill these things and they'll pick back up wherever they left off.
cards.claim: Because state lives in the plan file and git, a loop can be killed and restarted without loss.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex killed and restarted loops during the stream.
cards.landing: Phase routine resume design (cold-resume): state in repo files, not in the session

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I saw it rewrite the Alexa and PA like so many times and I thought the model was the issue.
cards.claim: A wrong spec (one keyword defined twice) made the loop tear down and rebuild the lexer repeatedly; the cause was garbage in, not the model, and a bad spec multiplies into thousands of bad lines.
cards.evidence_detail: Cursed lang run, Geoff speaking and Dex agreeing; 'one bad spec is like 10,000 lines of crap'.
cards.landing: Spec/plan review before dispatching an unattended phase; verifier on the plan, not just the diff

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the harness gets about a 16k overhead. You only got about 176k usable
cards.claim: Of a 200k window, roughly 16k goes to harness overhead leaving about 176k usable, and tool output, specs and prompts consume it quickly (a 136 KB movie script is about 60k tokens).
cards.evidence_detail: Rough figures from the guest's tokenisation; the 16k overhead number is said without a source.
cards.landing: Context budget: count the fixed load of CLAUDE.md plus skills per session

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: agents MD which should only be about 60 lines of uh code by the way.
cards.claim: Keep agents.md around 60 lines and tokenise your rules to see their cost; everything should be small to maximise time in the smart zone.
cards.evidence_detail: Closing advice; no data. The 60-line figure is said in passing.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim: a concrete target (390 lines vs about 60)

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Anthropic says it's important to shout at the LLM. GPT5 says if you shout at it
cards.claim: Prompt emphasis (shouting, capitals) is model-specific and can detune some models, so read each vendor's prompting guide.
cards.evidence_detail: Geoff's remark, Dex expands on tokenizer inspection and turning JSON into denser plain text.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md style audit: remove emphasis markers

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Loom is the encapsulation of some of these ideas
cards.claim: Geoff's Loom (remote ephemeral sandbox harness with a chain of agents poking agents: did you do X) is where the nudge pattern gets built in as infrastructure; Dex expresses interest, not adoption.
cards.evidence_detail: Geoff describes it as built in three days; no data.
cards.landing: Chained verifier agents that poke the builder; a workflow library

cards.source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Now these things will pull in any GitHub issues that get open.
cards.claim: Dex feeds a 'known issues' folder and live GitHub issues into the loop as inputs next to the specs, and jokes that issues could prompt-inject the loop.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed in the live stream when a flatten-directories bug was found.
cards.landing: Register ids as loop inputs; also an injection risk to name

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The bash loop was nice because I started to see common failure domains
cards.claim: Do not prompt the model to keep working; bound each run to one step and exit, and rerun it, so the work is bounded and the failure modes become visible and fixable.
cards.evidence_detail: Episode README: 'One-loop, one-step. Exit. Rerun.' Dex's own 'models get anxiety and terminate early' framing.
cards.landing: Phase routine: one bounded step per session instead of 'keep going'

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The models get anxiety model, it will terminate early.
cards.claim: Prompts that beg the model not to stop do not work; the way to get long work is short bounded runs repeated.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex cites a community talk whose whole prompt was 'do not stop after one step'.
cards.landing: Phase routine: avoid mega-prompts; rely on repo state for continuity

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the more context you use the worse results you'll get
cards.claim: Context budget plan: about 7% for specs, 7% for finding current state, 3% for the plan, 10-15% for base message and MCPs, leaving only roughly 10% for the work itself.
cards.evidence_detail: Numbers attributed to Geoff, repeated by Dex as a model; no experiment.
cards.landing: Per-phase context budget table in the ship plan

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the most high performance range I found for the models is like before you hit this 30 to 40%
cards.claim: Dex puts the high-performance range before about 30-40% of context fill; beyond it you are in the dumb zone, worse with many MCP tools loaded.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal observation; he concedes newer models are less affected but says less context still wins.
cards.landing: Session-length alarm / one-phase-per-session justification

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: No one will deny that you get better results if you use less
cards.claim: Even as models support longer windows, less context still gives better results because attention is spread over less noise; the dumb-zone effect is weakening but not gone.
cards.evidence_detail: Debate with Geoff and Vaibhav; Dex's counter-opinion is that long-context training is improving.
cards.landing: Context policy that does not rely on a single dumb-zone percentage

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The model will find something to do because you've invoked the cloud CLI
cards.claim: When the desired and current state match, a looped model still invents new work, usually by changing the desired state (adding types nobody specified), so completion needs an external stop.
cards.evidence_detail: Example: after ~100 loops it added types to the language implementation plan.
cards.landing: Completion criteria in the plan; verifier that rejects scope growth

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Don't mix the concerns.
cards.claim: Appending unrelated tasks to one conversation (change colour, then SQL migration) degrades results; one item per context window gives good outcomes.
cards.evidence_detail: Geoff's observation, Dex restates it as the reason Ralph works.
cards.landing: One phase per new session

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Back pressure is your governor. Strong typing or strong checks make the loop honest.
cards.claim: Back pressure (types, tests, build, lint, scanners) is what stops bad generation; the weaker the checks, the more engineering is needed to wire them in, and the loop's speed is limited by the slowest check.
cards.evidence_detail: README key idea; the C to Rust to Zig experience with the cursed compiler (C had none and went backwards).
cards.landing: CI gates as backpressure: mypy, import-linter, alembic check; wire them into agent-visible commands

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: They'll spend three days designing the back pressure harness
cards.claim: Dex repeats that the best agentic engineers spend days designing how the model will know it is working, then hand it over to run for ~48 hours.
cards.evidence_detail: Said as a general claim about top practitioners; 50,000 lines is an illustrative figure.
cards.landing: Phase 0 of any long task: design the verifier before the work

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Note: This is a conceptual exploration. It's not 'do this for your production app today.'
cards.claim: The episode frames Ralph as a mental model, not a production recipe; use when you have a crisp spec and fast checks, avoid when work needs long contiguous context with weak feedback or human review at every step.
cards.evidence_detail: Episode README 'when to use it' lists; the quote is from the README, written by the episode team.
cards.landing: Criteria for when a phase may run unattended

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can get into the high 70s 80s. Like there's going to be holes.
cards.claim: Unattended loops reach roughly 70-95% of a spec; output cannot be trusted when it says done, and review is the new bottleneck.
cards.evidence_detail: Geoff says 'high 70s, 80s' and 'when it says it's done, it's not really done'; Dex says 90-95% with steering.
cards.landing: Treat self-reported completion as unverified; verifier required

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Engineering has professional liability to it.
cards.claim: Geoff's closing position that the engineer stays accountable for AI-generated code and cannot blame the tool; Dex does not dispute it.
cards.evidence_detail: Closing remark.
cards.landing: Owner view: the named human sign-off per phase

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're actually malicking and burning a lot of tokens so it can just do that one thing
cards.claim: Re-allocating the same context each iteration is deliberately token-inefficient; the cost trade is accepted for determinism and smart-zone work, and a stable prefix could be cached.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex notes @-mentioning the plan in the user message defeats prompt caching; cost not quantified here.
cards.landing: Cost model for fresh-session-per-phase; keep the stable prefix first for caching

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: anything that was a minty allocation like cargo test
cards.claim: Geoff: run noisy commands (cargo test) in sub-agents so only the exit code returns to the main context, comparable to garbage-collected green threads.
cards.evidence_detail: Geoff's account; Dex does not push back.
cards.landing: Run test and build commands via a subagent or quiet wrapper

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you'd throw away the implementation plan continually because it was so easy to regenerate
cards.claim: If a loop hill-climbs without arriving, discard and regenerate the plan rather than patching it; code and plans are disposable, ideas and specs carry the value.
cards.evidence_detail: Geoff's practice; README states 'Code is disposable'.
cards.landing: Plan lifecycle: regenerate the phase plan when the journal shows drift

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: for extremely extremely hard tasks what I need to worry about at all times is the model will not continue
cards.claim: Weakness of the technique, stated by the co-host and accepted by Dex: tasks needing long context horizon suffer because the implementation plan lacks detail, so the loop is a poor fit there.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's summary of the tradeoff; Dex and Geoff accept it.
cards.landing: Gating rule: which phases are loop-suitable versus interactive

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: there's forward modes, there's research modes, and there's reverse modes.
cards.claim: Loop modes: forward (specs to code), research (study the source versus specs to write a gap plan), and reverse (code to specs), each using the same desired-state versus current-state frame.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex demonstrates a reverse-mode prompt for a Go to TypeScript port.
cards.landing: Saved workflow variants: audit loop (research mode) writing a gap register

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Ralph as control loops: desired state, current state, take one action
cards.claim: Dex frames Ralph as a control loop (desired state, current state, one action, re-read) borrowed from Kubernetes controllers.
cards.evidence_detail: Conceptual framing in the episode; reappears as Kyle's control-theory talk.
cards.landing: Loop design vocabulary for the register-driven phase plan

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The best AI engineers constantly challenge their own worldview of what is happening.
cards.claim: Vaibhav's remark that practitioners must keep re-testing what the model can now do; Dex sets up the topic on this basis. Counted only as Dex's framing for running the episode.
cards.evidence_detail: Co-host statement; low weight.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: we're still building 40,000 line PRs that just nobody wants to read
cards.claim: Kyle argues that piping a prompt to an agent in a loop, even with many verifiers and review agents, yields unreadable giant PRs; blind Ralph suits solo or non-critical work, not teams with SLAs.
cards.evidence_detail: Conference talk framing.
cards.landing: PR-size cap and reviewability as a loop output constraint

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: we can design loops and still read the code.
cards.claim: Position: loops should make code easier to read and keep humans reading it, against the 'read-only code, invest in verification' view of frontier labs.
cards.evidence_detail: Contrasts a conference thesis that code will be unread; notes Claude Code flicker took 6 months to fix.
cards.landing: Owner view: the human still reviews; loops produce small PRs

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: this is really expensive if you don't work at a Frontier Lab
cards.claim: Kyle says the read-nothing, loop-everything approach is expensive without an unlimited token budget, and bad code costs more in the agent era.
cards.evidence_detail: No numbers given; cites Matt Pocock.
cards.landing: Cost-awareness for unattended loops

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: control loops change a system incrementally instead of just trying to get straight to the end state
cards.claim: Agentic control loop = set point, sensor, controller, actuator; incremental change with measured error avoids over-steering; a blind Ralph loop has no controller bounding the step.
cards.evidence_detail: Control-theory exposition with thermostat, Kubernetes, Postgres autovacuum examples.
cards.landing: Workflow template: sensor, pick-one, actuate, PR

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: I don't think you should ever send an agent to do deterministic code's job
cards.claim: Use deterministic sensors and selection (ast-grep, ESLint, bash and jq to pick the first or smallest violation) rather than an agent wherever the job is deterministic.
cards.evidence_detail: Worked example: migrating RPC procedures to Effect, picking the smallest unmigrated one.
cards.landing: Scripted checks for harness compliance (e.g. ast-grep for slice boundaries) rather than prose rules

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: watched Claude disable those with inline comments.
cards.claim: ast-grep is useful as a sensor because it sits out of band from TypeScript config or ESLint rules, which agents are seen disabling with inline comments.
cards.evidence_detail: Observation by Kyle.
cards.landing: Verifier independence: a gate the agent cannot edit away

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: run a full scan once on main, sort all the violations deterministically
cards.claim: Baseline the violation list in version control and, on every PR, check the branch adds no new violations (a 'disturbance dampener') so teammates do not undo the loop's work.
cards.evidence_detail: Used in the Effect migration at HumanLayer.
cards.landing: Ratchet CI check: counted baseline file for known defect shapes

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: build out what we call golden patterns by hand before setting the agent loose
cards.claim: Hand-write idiomatic example patterns for the actuator skill to follow, because agents replicate patterns; iterate the skill over time, not all up front.
cards.evidence_detail: HumanLayer practice, no numbers.
cards.landing: Skills with golden examples (outbox kind, slice router, migration)

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: we're going to deterministically commit and push and create a PR
cards.claim: The loop ends with a deterministic commit, push and PR creation, using the agent's final response template as the PR description; run it from CI (GitHub Actions) on a daily schedule for one small PR per morning.
cards.evidence_detail: Described as their internal setup; no numbers.
cards.landing: PR-open step done by a script; scheduled agents for maintenance loops

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: create a feedback file that's tracked in version control just as a markdown file
cards.claim: Steer a loop with a tracked feedback.md loaded into every run; a '/iterate' PR comment loads the diff and comments and has the agent fix the code and update the feedback file.
cards.evidence_detail: Added after the first version was too high-friction and was switched off.
cards.landing: Decisions journal as a loaded input; owner correction path via PR comment

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: exactly one PR at most open per loop at a time
cards.claim: Flow control: a loop exits at start if any PR carrying its label is still open, since no human has reviewed the last output, so work never stacks on unreviewed work.
cards.evidence_detail: Introduced after loop PRs piled up and conflicted while the team was away.
cards.landing: Gate: no new phase starts while the prior phase's PR is unreviewed

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: each migration gets its own context window
cards.claim: Scale a loop by picking 3-5 items per run but doing each in a separate implementation phase with its own context (cheaper and more reliable), or by running it several times for different people; at 150 procedures one-per-day would take 6 months.
cards.evidence_detail: Calculation from the 150-procedure example.
cards.landing: Batch size per session; fan-out of fresh-context workers

cards.source_title: Loops Engineering from First Principles
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: depending on the complexity, we could have the agent pick the procedure to migrate and just do it
cards.claim: The controller can feed the actuator extra signal (telemetry on error-prone or uninstrumented procedures) so the change improves the code rather than doing a one-to-one port.
cards.evidence_detail: Suggested extension, not shown running.
cards.landing: Ops telemetry as input to prioritising which fix a loop picks

cards.source_title: HumanLayer Collaboration Demo
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: artifacts are basically these documents that are used for alignment with the model
cards.claim: HumanLayer artifacts (design and plan documents) accumulate on the task alongside sessions, can be commented on by teammates and streamed code is reviewable while the agent works, instead of a chat or a late PR.
cards.evidence_detail: Product walkthrough with no numbers.
cards.landing: Plan and decisions journal as reviewable shared documents; early review of in-progress code

cards.source_title: HumanLayer Collaboration Demo
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you could pick a workflow. This is unique to Human Layer. You can use RPI or Crispy.
cards.claim: The product offers named workflows (RPI, CRISPY, PRD, free form) chosen when a task starts, with model, effort and attached context set per session.
cards.evidence_detail: UI description; effort is a per-session setting.
cards.landing: Workflow selection at phase start; effort set per session

gaps: Dev Interrupted (LinearB) Ralph economics episode: no transcript or file was in my bundle and I did not fetch it, so the ~$10-11/hour Sonnet figure and Dex's position on loop cost are not carded.

The Showdown stream and AITW transcripts are auto-captions with many mishearings (e.g. 'malicking' is 'malloc-ing', 'Lexa and PA' is 'lexer and parser', 'chord code' is 'Claude Code'); quotes are verbatim as captioned.

The Showdown stream's second half (after the loop restarts) has no final results; the outcome comparison of plugin versus bash loop is only partial (plugin had fewer tests, bash loop kept finding work).

In the AITW episode much of the loop technique is voiced by Geoff Huntley; cards R17-24, R17-32, R17-35, R17-36, R17-37 record his statements that Dex repeats or does not dispute, with weaker adoption evidence than Dex's own claims.
The Collaboration Demo is a 90-second product walkthrough, so there are no loop-gating positions in it.
No measured data (token counts, cost, pass rates) appears in any of the four videos beyond rough figures (16k/176k window, 60k tokens per script, 30-40% zone, 7/7/3/10-15% budget).
